### FR-FLOW-136 — A verification ledger scopes prose re-review to changed sections

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 2.12.0-verification-economy |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | medium |
| Tags | 2.12.0, verification-ledger, verification-economy |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | docs/research/19.verification-token-economy-research.md |

#### Requirement

The document review loop SHALL record verified prose sections in a heading-keyed, content-hash ledger at `kiwi/verification-ledger.jsonl` and pass only dirty sections — hash-changed or ledger-unmatched — to the verifier subagent with surrounding context, so a review round reads what changed instead of the whole document. An unmatched heading key is always dirty, failing open toward re-verification rather than toward false trust, and one full-document audit remains mandatory before the target closes because a section can be individually true yet false in a changed surrounding context.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: A section's identity is its heading path and its hash is computed over the normalized section body, so reflowing whitespace, changing line endings or shifting line numbers does not dirty it while any wording change does. Normalization collapses whitespace only — it must not strip markdown or punctuation, or two sections that differ meaningfully collide.
- [x] AC-2: A round sends the verifier only sections whose hash differs from the ledger or whose heading key has no ledger entry; a clean section is not sent and carries no payload. A renamed or split heading is unmatched and therefore dirty. Because the key is the heading PATH, renaming a parent dirties every descendant — the fail-open direction the design asks for, at a cost stated here rather than discovered later.
- [x] AC-3: The ledger is an append-only JSONL file at kiwi/verification-ledger.jsonl recording section key, hash, verifier identity and round. Pruning an orphan appends a tombstone record rather than deleting a line: the entry leaves the folded state while the line that recorded it remains on disk, because a file cannot be both append-only and edited. Pruning is idempotent, and a heading that returns with identical text is dirty rather than resurrected clean.
- [x] AC-4: Pruning happens on each planning pass — the operation a review round actually runs — not on an orchestrator pass, because the consuming skill is invoked by the orchestrator and has no pass of its own.
- [x] AC-5: The hash is computed by the tool, never by the calling agent, and the ledger is written through a command surface the skill can execute; an agent-asserted hash is not evidence. A record call stores the tool's hash of the current text, not a hash supplied by the caller.
- [x] AC-6: The skill that owns the ledger requires one full-document audit that ignores the ledger before the requirements it reviewed are closed, and states the limitation in the shipped text: a section can be individually true yet false in a changed surrounding context, hash-clean sections are not re-read, and that cross-section dependency is knowingly traded for the token saving. Where the close is performed by a skill that reviews only code, that skill does not close a requirement whose verification evidence rests on prose; it reports the omission instead, because an obligation a skill cannot discharge is not a gate.

AC-1 asserts both directions — reflow, CRLF and trailing whitespace keep a section clean, a prepended section that shifts every line number keeps it clean, one changed word dirties it — plus a guard that the normalizer is not over-aggressive, so `- **enabled** by default` and `- enabled by default`, and `value is 10` and `value is 100`, must not collide. AC-2 asserts a clean section is absent from the sent set AND carries no payload; renamed, split, empty-verifier and duplicate-heading cases all dirty. AC-3 asserts append-only as afterPrune.startsWith(afterFirst) and strictly longer, prune appends exactly one tombstone, is idempotent, and a heading that returns with identical text is dirty rather than resurrected. AC-6 was verified beforehand to be unsatisfiable by shipped text — `verification-ledger`, `전체 문서`, `교차 의존` and `장부` each occurred zero times across skills/** and .agents/skills/** — then asserted across all four copies of kiwi-review-fix-loop for an unhedged audit obligation carrying a count and naming the close it guards, and a limitation line naming the cross-section dependency in the words that make it a stated trade rather than an omission. Two corrections during implementation rather than after: one test expectation was wrong and was fixed instead of the code (a never-recorded section is correctly dirty, not skipped); and a post-green strengthening, red first at 'expected dirty to be clean', found that keying a document by its verbatim path makes `docs\\guide.md` and `docs/guide.md` two disjoint documents, so on Windows the ledger would silently never reuse anything — a fail-open producing no diagnostic. #### Requirement

A requirement whose implementation depends on a measured fact, a named seam, a trap, or a rejected alternative SHALL record it in the requirement block itself rather than only in a research file. The blueprint is the requirement, because that is what an implementer is given, what a reviewer checks against, and what a test can be tied to; a research file is a working note that may already be wrong.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: A measured fact an implementer must not re-derive is recorded with how it was measured, so a reader can re-run it rather than trust it. The rule exists because three counts inherited from a research file were wrong and were caught only when someone ran the code.
- [x] AC-2: A ground-truth choice that has a wrong-looking alternative is stated as a decision with its measurement, not left implicit. The anchor convention is the worked example: checking GitHub heading slugs instead of the explicit id tags this repository uses reports every link broken, so an implementer who re-derives the ground truth picks the one that fails.
- [x] AC-3: A trap on the implementation path is named where the implementer will read it. The worked example is a shared helper that discards its input argument: honouring that argument is the natural-looking fix and would open the entire SRS family, which no test the requirement asks for would catch.
- [x] AC-4: A rejected alternative is recorded with the reason and the condition that would reopen it, so the next session does not re-litigate it from scratch or silently reverse it.
- [x] AC-5: A requirement is not required to carry design it does not have. This criterion is satisfied by requirements with nothing to record, so the rule cannot be met by writing filler — the check is that what an implementer needed was written down, not that a section is non-empty.

#### Requirement

An agent given a requirement to implement SHALL be told that the requirement may itself be wrong, and SHALL report a conflict between the requirement and the code instead of implementing around it. This is where the real gate sits: research prose is not reviewed, so the requirement is the first thing an implementer can contradict with evidence, and the contradiction must reach the author rather than be quietly absorbed.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The instruction is present in the skills that hand an agent a requirement to implement, in all shipped variants, and names both halves: the requirement may be wrong, and a conflict is reported rather than worked around.
- [x] AC-2: The instruction is unhedged. A phrasing that merely permits reporting does not satisfy it — an agent that may report will implement around the conflict, because implementing is the task it was given.
- [x] AC-3: The instruction names what counts as a conflict concretely enough to act on: a fact the requirement asserts that the code contradicts, a criterion that cannot be satisfied as written, and a criterion that two parts of the same requirement answer differently. All three occurred this session.
- [x] AC-4: A reported conflict is resolved by amending the requirement or recording why it stands, never by silently satisfying the letter of a criterion the author would not recognise — the amendment is visible in the requirement's Change Notes.

The improve loop that follows the prickly review SHALL NOT spend a rework round on a finding whose subject is the wording or formatting of a comment. Such a finding SHALL remain reportable as information only. This is the cost the user named: the loop grants at least one senior-coder round to that severity, and the record contains no defect it has ever caught.

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

A rule written in only one of the two is contradicted by the other, and the budget table is the one an agent counts rounds from.
- [x] AC-2: A comment-wording observation stays reportable as information. Removing the reviewer's ability to say it at all would be a different change — a reviewer who cannot file an observation under its own name files it under another one, and it returns as a round somewhere else.

- [x] AC-4: The test that pins those severity lines by canonical equality is updated in the same commit as the skill. A rule the suite forbids is not in force, and the pin exists precisely so that changing the contract is deliberate rather than incidental.
- [x] AC-5: The generated mirror under .agents carries the change, produced by regenerating it rather than by hand-editing it — that mirror is the rendering agents actually read.

### FR-FLOW-141 — A comment does not cite a location or a count that moves without it

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 2.12.0-review-cost |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | high |
| Tags | - |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | - |

#### Requirement

A comment in this repository's sources SHALL NOT cite a location by absolute line number, and SHALL NOT restate a count of a set that is enumerated elsewhere. Both are claims that go false when something unrelated is edited, and each one that exists is verification work whose only product is re-deriving a number. A comment SHALL instead name what it points at in terms that move with it: a symbol, a heading title, or a Requirement ID with its criterion.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: A mechanical check rejects an absolute line-number citation written in a comment under the source trees, reporting the offending file, line and citation. The check reads files itself rather than shelling out to a text search, because five files in these trees carry NUL bytes and a text search drops them silently.
- [x] AC-2: The trees are clean when the check is introduced, so it cannot ship inert. Every citation that exists on the day it lands is either converted to a form that moves with its subject or exempted at its own line, and the exemption is visible where the check reads it rather than declared once for a whole file.
- [x] AC-3: The replacement forms are named where an authoring agent reads them, so the rule tells the author what to write instead of only what not to write: a code symbol, a document heading title, or a Requirement ID with its criterion.
- [x] AC-4: The rule that a count of an enumerated set is not restated beside it is stated in every shipped variant of the authoring instructions and in the generated mirror. Where the set can be reached from the assertion, the count is derived from it rather than written down.
- [x] AC-5: The check does not fire on a line number that is data rather than a citation — a diagnostic's reported position, a fixture, a parsed result. Those are values the code computes, and forbidding them would make the rule unusable in the parser and mutation tests that form the bulk of this suite.

Conversion measured that four citations in one file (src/core/orchestrator/auto-gate.ts) already pointed at the wrong sections, and one named a line past the end of the document it cited. AC-5 is proved by cases asserting a bare position in prose and a line number in code are both ignored. The check found its own illustrative example on first green run, which is how the same-line exemption earned its place. |

### FR-FLOW-142 — SRS verification does not iterate against an unverified document

| GitHub Issue | - |

#### Requirement

The verification loop that compares an authored SRS against a research document SHALL stop on severity rather than on the exhaustion of findings, and SHALL NOT scale its verification fan-out by the number of research documents. A research document is an unverified working note, so a loop that iterates until it raises no finding at all is converging on a standard nothing has established, and it pays for every round with real subagents.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The loop's exit condition names a severity floor rather than the absence of findings. An exit that requires zero findings of any kind cannot be reached by evidence over prose, so in practice the loop always runs to its divergence guard and the guard becomes the real cost.
- [x] AC-2: The verification fan-out is not multiplied by the number of research documents. The per-document multiplier is the largest single cost in this loop and it buys cross-checking of a document that carries no authority, since research is declared unverified.
- [x] AC-3: The severity gate on the requirements themselves is untouched. This requirement removes rounds spent comparing prose against prose; it does not lower the bar on an acceptance criterion, a contract, or a safety boundary, all of which keep the full policy.
- [x] AC-4: The stated divergence guard and the stated fan-out agree with each other and with the loop's exit condition wherever each is written, including the skill's own summary description — a cost stated in one place and contradicted in another is read as whichever the agent meets first.
- [x] AC-5: The change is present in every shipped variant and in the generated mirror, produced by regenerating the mirror rather than editing it.

### FR-FLOW-143 — A verification axis whose rule is decidable runs as a script, not as an agent

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 2.12.0-review-cost |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | high |
| Tags | - |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | - |

#### Requirement

A TDD verification axis whose pass rule is stated as a set membership, a string comparison, a regular expression, or a build result SHALL be evaluated by a shipped script rather than by a subagent. The axes covered are req-mapping and red-verification. The guarantee each axis carries is unchanged; what changes is that a decidable rule stops being executed by a judge, which is both cheaper and stricter — a string comparison admits no near-miss.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The req-mapping rule is evaluated by REUSING the shipped plan validator that already decides it, not by a second implementation. That validator already checks that a test case's requirement id belongs to the task's requirement set, that its criterion references are a subset of the requirement's criteria, and that its identifier matches the declared pattern. A reimplementation would be a second place for the same rule to drift.
- [x] AC-2: The red-verification rule is decided mechanically rather than by a judge: the authored test is executed and its exit status and failure signature are compared against the declared expectation by equality. An approximate match is a failure — this is stricter than the judgement it replaces, and that strictness is the point. Unlike req-mapping this is an inline comparison rather than a separate shipped file, and the requirement does not claim otherwise.
- [x] AC-3: The reused validator is proved to decide, by running it: a plan whose test case names a requirement outside its task's set, one whose criterion references fall outside that requirement, and one whose identifier is malformed each make it report the corresponding violation, while a clean plan passes. Asserting that the rule's name appears in the file proves only that a string is present; running it is what shows the reuse is real.
- [x] AC-4: The skill no longer spawns a subagent for either axis, in every shipped variant and the generated mirror, and the axis count it states agrees with the number of agent-evaluated axes that remain. A count left stale contradicts the table beneath it.
- [x] AC-5: The guarantee is not weakened anywhere it is relied upon: the pass gate still requires the red evidence, the evidence record carries the same fields it carried before, and the verdicts the moved axes now produce still block the phase rather than advising it. Each is asserted against the line that carries it, not against the document — a phrase found anywhere proves nothing about the rule that uses it.
- [x] AC-6: The reuse is self-contained: the skill invokes the validator for the task it is working on AND states where the validator's required input comes from, because it can be entered on a plan authored elsewhere. Naming the invocation while leaving its input to an upstream step reproduces the same defect one argument further in — the check runs, refuses for want of an input nobody was told to make, and the axis fails for a reason unrelated to the code.

Measured — req-mapping is stated as set membership and a regex, red-verification as exit status plus signature equality. intent-alignment and technical-quality are NOT, and stay with agents. Do not extend this requirement to them; that question went to a decision committee separately.

The floor protects the CHECK, not the agent that runs it — moving it to a script keeps the floor and tightens it, since equality admits no near-miss where a judge might accept one. The axis was an agent re-deciding what a script had decided. AC-6 exists because the skill can start from a plan that validator never saw.

#### Requirement

The formal check that follows implementation SHALL be evaluated by a shipped script rather than by a subagent. Three of its four axes restate rules the repository already decides mechanically. The fourth names a subject without stating any rule at all, so this requirement SHALL define that rule rather than pretend to relocate one — a check whose criterion was never written cannot be moved, only written.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The three restated axes are evaluated by reusing what already decides them rather than by reimplementing: the mock prohibition uses the existing pattern, the type and build axis uses the build, and the plan-code mapping axis reuses the result the preceding mechanical gate already computed. A second implementation of the same rule is a second place for it to drift.
- [x] AC-2: The coverage axis is given an explicit rule, stated in the skill where a reader meets the axis: every test case the task declares corresponds to a test that actually executed. This is chosen over a global percentage because it decides what the task promised rather than what the repository averages, and because a percentage has no defined threshold anywhere in the skill today.
- [x] AC-3: The absence being repaired is recorded where it will be read, so a later reader does not mistake a newly written rule for a relocated one. The record names what was missing: no criterion for the coverage axis existed in the skill or in its extended reference.
- [x] AC-4: Each of the four rules is asserted individually, and removing any one of them turns the check red. The formal check is a rule set stated in the skill rather than a separate shipped file, so this is the mutation proof the artefact admits: a fixture cannot be fed to a script that does not exist as one, but a rule silently dropped from the set can and must be caught.
- [x] AC-5: The skill no longer spawns a subagent for the formal check, in every shipped variant and the generated mirror, and no surviving sentence still describes it as a subagent pass.

#### Requirement

A skill that declares it honours the shared round-cap options SHALL bind those options to the loop bound it actually evaluates. A declaration that sits beside a hardcoded literal is not a contract, because the literal is what runs — the flag reads as supported, changes nothing, and the discrepancy is invisible to anyone who only reads the declaration.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

#### Requirement

Where a skill states a rule twice, the two statements SHALL agree, and where a skill grants a repeatable action it SHALL state the bound on repetition. An agent reads whichever statement it meets first, so a contradiction is not an inconsistency to tidy later — it is two different behaviours shipping under one name. An unbounded repetition is the same defect with no second statement to compare against.

#### Rationale

-

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The contradiction over which model a scope-authoring subagent uses is resolved to one answer, and the losing statement is removed rather than left to be reconciled by a reader. Two surviving statements that merely no longer contradict are still two places to drift.
- [x] AC-2: The subagent whose re-spawn had no stated bound is given one, and the bound is named where the re-spawn is granted. A retry loop with no ceiling is unbounded cost wearing the appearance of a safeguard.
- [x] AC-3: The mode multiplier whose meaning was never defined — whether it means concurrent instances or a strengthened exit condition — is defined, and the definition distinguishes the two so the reader cannot pick the cheaper reading by accident.
- [x] AC-4: The round-cap options are mapped to the specific counters they replace, rather than declared to replace unnamed ones. Which counter a flag bounds is what an agent needs to act; a declaration that names no counter cannot be followed.
- [x] AC-5: Each repair is asserted mechanically over every shipped variant and the generated mirror, so a fix applied to one rendering and not another is caught rather than assumed.

A verification pass that a skill spawns SHALL persist its findings to the run's artifact directory. Without that record, a pass that has caught nothing is indistinguishable from a pass that was rarely run and from one whose output was discarded — and a repository cannot decide whether a check earns its cost when it cannot tell those three apart.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-4: The rule is stated in every shipped variant and the generated mirror.

#### Requirement

The `kiwi-orchestrator` skill body SHALL declare, in its critical gate table and in all shipped variants, the wall-clock run budget gate and the subagent budget gate, and the budget option descriptions SHALL name the gate each one raises.

#### Rationale

A gate the code can express but the skill never names is unreachable in practice: the agent writes the abort line, and it writes what the body told it to write. The body currently describes both budget exhaustions as ending the run at the next stage boundary without saying what to put in `abort_gate`, so the agent has nothing to name and the append is refused. The skill's own rule cuts both ways here — it warns that declaring a gate with no predicate behind it is worse than omitting it, and the inverse is what this closes: a predicate that fires with no declared name.

- [x] AC-4: The `--subagent-budget` option description names the gate it raises, and keeps the existing round verdict and reason class it already specifies.
- [x] AC-5: Both declarations are present in every shipped variant of the skill.
- [x] AC-6: Both declared identifiers are members of the code-side gate union, so the declared-subset-of-union property holds.

### FR-FLOW-150 — The lane plan lock has one path and the skill passes it explicitly

#### Requirement

The `kiwi-orchestrator` skill body SHALL spell the lane plan lock at exactly one path, per wave, in every place it names the file, and SHALL pass that path explicitly on every command that reads or writes it rather than relying on a tool default.

#### Rationale

The body spells the file three different ways — under the wave directory in the fixed-path convention, under a run-scoped orchestrator directory in the worktree procedure, and the tool's own default is a fourth spelling with no wave in it. Nothing in the body says which wins. The lock is content-addressed and re-frozen per wave, and a re-freeze that reads one spelling and writes another produces a drift refusal whose stated cause (recomputed plan differs) is not the real one (two files). The per-wave spelling is the one the semantics require: the plan is re-frozen at each wave close and is the denominator of that wave's verification, so a run-scoped or wave-less path would have later waves overwrite earlier ones.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: Every mention in the skill body that states a location for the lane plan lock — that is, one carrying a directory component — uses the same wave-scoped path.
- [x] AC-2: The worktree procedure section states that same path rather than a run-scoped one.
- [x] AC-3: Every command invocation in the body that reads or writes the lock passes the path explicitly, so no tool default is relied on.
- [x] AC-4: The single spelling is identical across all shipped variants of the skill.
- [x] AC-5: No stated location omits the wave component, since that would let a later wave overwrite an earlier one.
- [x] AC-6: A mention that names the artifact without stating where it lives stays a bare file name, because prefixing a noun with a path adds no location information and would break `FR-FLOW-084` AC-3, which pins that reference.

The producing call is now stated at the verb that writes the lock, and the test requires both the flag and the wave-scoped path in that stanza. #### Requirement

The `kiwi-orchestrator` skill body SHALL state, for the epic probe field, that linked sub-issues are counted by parsing the issue body's checklist references, and SHALL NOT name a producer the issue-viewing surface does not provide.

#### Rationale

The probe row names a single producer for the epic field and the routing rule then reads a linked sub-issue count from it, but that count has no producer: the issue-view JSON field list contains no sub-issue field, and the sub-issue endpoint returns zero for the meta issues this rule exists to catch. Measured on a real tracking issue carrying 77 checklist items across three groups: the native sub-issue total was 0 while every one of the 77 lines carried a leading issue reference. The routing verdict happens to come out right today because the same rule also counts task-list groups, but the body promises an observation it cannot make, and a probe that records an unobtainable field as unreadable fails closed and removes a rung. The rule that no predicate may read a value absent from the probe makes this a contract defect rather than a wording nit.

### FR-FLOW-152 — The code review loop selects its targets by file class, not by the path that produced them

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 3.0.1 |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | high |
| Tags | - |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | - |

#### Requirement

The code review loop SHALL select its review targets by file class, applying that filter to the candidate list its scope algorithm produces and before any reviewer subagent is spawned. Source files, test files and named configuration files are targets; prose is not. The commit-window flags SHALL NOT exempt a file from the filter, because the orchestrator's own terminal hop passes a window containing the run artifacts it committed moments earlier, which is the path by which research and design prose actually entered review. An explicit file list is a person naming files and is honoured for the code among them, while the prose among them is reported as excluded rather than silently dropped or quietly reviewed.

#### Rationale

Reported by the user: the loop rewrites documents the tool did not author, and it grew more frequent with more capable models. The mechanism is not the working-tree branch of the scope algorithm. The orchestrator commits its run artifacts under docs/research/{work}/ on its own schedule and then hands that commit range to the review loop as --base/--head, so those documents arrive through the highest-priority explicit-argument path. A more capable reviewer reading that window finds more to fix in it, which is why capability made the symptom worse rather than better. A fix covering only the working-tree path leaves the actual route open.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The target classes are stated as a closed list rather than as the adjective code, and the text names the three cases that are otherwise read the wrong way: a test file is code, a named configuration file is code, and a comment inside a code file is code. A copy carrying only the adjective does not satisfy this, because an adjective is something a reader argues with and a closed list is not.
- [x] AC-2: The commit-window flags (--base/--head, --commits, --since) do not exempt a file from the class filter, and the text states why: the orchestrator's terminal hop passes a window containing the run artifacts committed under its own schedule. Only an explicit --files list counts as a person naming a file, and prose named there is excluded and reported rather than reviewed.
- [x] AC-3: Excluded prose is enumerated in full in the run own artifact and in its report rather than summarised, and the count identity holds across four buckets: every candidate is either included, listed as excluded prose, listed as a refused run artifact, or listed as unclassified. Three buckets did not exhaust the candidates and two never held at all. The journals and locks the ordering rule refuses first are neither code nor prose, and the orchestrator commits them inside the very window this loop is handed; binaries and assets are neither either. A bucket short, the identity fails on the main path and the signal it exists to give becomes noise. The unclassified bucket carries a name that does not collide with the finding-classification value of the same word, which is forbidden and gated at zero in this skill.
- [x] AC-4: When the class filter leaves no code target, the loop stops instead of reporting a pass. A run that reviewed nothing does not record a passing quality gate, because an empty baseline reports clean for the same reason a clean one does.
- [x] AC-5: The boundary is carried in the skill's description front matter and not only in its body, because an agent reads the description when it chooses the skill and reads the body only after it has chosen.
- [x] AC-6: doc_only is removed from the TDD-exemption reason enum. Leaving it lets a fixer that edited prose claim exemption and proceed straight to the fix phase, which is the cheapest way around this requirement.
- [x] AC-7: A path naming a run journal or a lock is refused before the class filter is consulted, and that ordering is stated in the text. Without the stated ordering, the rule that a named configuration file is code admits waves.jsonl, resume-card.json and the route locks, which are structurally JSON.
- [x] AC-8: All four shipped copies carry the rules: skills/claude, skills/codex, skills/etc and the .agents mirror. A rule present in three of four leaves one host on the old contract.
- [x] AC-9: The halt on an empty code scope collides with the orchestrator terminal hop when every candidate is prose, and that limitation is written into the shipped text rather than left to be rediscovered from a stuck run. The text names what collides, why this section cannot resolve it (the exemption branch keys on an empty commit window, and widening that predicate belongs to the requirement that owns it), and that the resolution is deferred. Recording a bounded gap is a legitimate outcome here; recording it only in a test while the requirement stays silent is not, because a reader would then see eight criteria all satisfied and no trace of the named path that cannot complete.

### FR-FLOW-153 — The prohibition on reviewing research prose reaches the shipped skills

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 3.0.1 |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | high |
| Tags | - |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | - |

#### Requirement

The shipped skill text SHALL carry the prohibition on running a verify-and-improve loop over research prose, at each place where such a loop actually reads that prose, together with the reason and a pointer to the requirement that states the rule in full. The prohibition already exists as a verified requirement, but its only enforcement point is this repository's own policy file, which the package does not distribute; a rule that reaches no installed project is in force nowhere but here.

#### Rationale

FR-FLOW-137 states that no review loop is to be run over research prose and is Status=verified, yet its AC-3 checks the verification intensity policy in CLAUDE.md and nothing checks the skills. A search for that prohibition across skills/** returns zero occurrences. The gap is not theoretical: on 2026-08-22, five days after FR-FLOW-137 was verified, commits 39fb90e and 5bf4434 revised research prose in response to review findings in this very repository. An installed project has neither the policy file nor the skill rule, so it has nothing at all. This requirement is not new policy; it is the wiring repair for a requirement that already passed.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: The prohibition appears in the shipped text at each place a loop actually reads research prose: the shared verification engine _shared/kiwi/verify-loop.md, which the orchestrator and wave-master both cite, and the SRS authoring skill's research-driven A/B loop. All four distributed copies of each carry it. A skill whose loop reads only code is out of scope, because the line there would be a rule with no subject.
- [x] AC-2: The prohibition is stated with its reason rather than as a bare rule: a research document is an unverified working note, and a loop that polishes it makes it read as verified, so the next reader stands on it as fact. A line that only forbids without saying why is re-litigated by the next capable model.
- [x] AC-3: FR-FLOW-137 is named in the same passage as the prohibition, not merely somewhere in the file. The SRS skill already cites that requirement while arguing about a termination condition, so a check that only looks for the identifier anywhere in the text passes on shipped prose that forbids nothing.
- [x] AC-4: The check reads the distributed text, not the policy file. An assertion satisfied by CLAUDE.md alone does not satisfy this requirement, because CLAUDE.md is not part of the package and the distance between the two is the defect being repaired.

The red count is stated carefully because a verifier caught the first version overstating it: the 20 observed were taken after the engine half had already been written, and restoring all eight files to HEAD gives 40. AC-3 requires the identifier inside the prohibition passage rather than anywhere in the file, and the window reads FORWARD from the prohibition — reading backward let the pre-existing kiwi-srs sentence satisfy the assertion, which the verifier demonstrated by deleting the new citation and staying green. AC-1 separates forbidding from describing, and the negation is matched together with the verb: a bare match on the verb was satisfied by a permission, and replacing the whole prohibition with one stayed green until it was fixed. The one that stays green moves the section to the top of the same file, which the AC does not forbid — it asks for the rule in each FILE where a loop reads prose, and position inside the file carries no meaning when the whole text loads at once. Wired into the shared verification engine (kiwi-orchestrator and kiwi-wave-master both cite it) and into the SRS skill's process A, whose body lives in SKILL.md for claude and in references/extended-workflow.md for the other renderings. |

### FR-FLOW-154 — Skill text names only status and stability values the code defines, and a contract test holds it there

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 3.1.0 |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | critical |
| Tags | plan-3.0-01, audit-28 |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | docs/plan/3.0/01.status-enum-contract.md, docs/research/28.skills-mcp-end-to-end-audit.md |

#### Requirement

Every requirement-status value that the shipped skill text names SHALL be a member of `REQUIREMENT_STATUSES`, and every requirement-stability value it names SHALL be a member of `STABILITY_LEVELS`, across all three renderings and the mirror. A contract test SHALL walk the renderings and fail when either set gains a member the code does not define, so that a later edit reintroducing one is caught by the suite rather than by a validation error in a consumer repository. The skill text and the code constants are two copies of one contract; today neither checks the other, and this requirement makes the code copy authoritative and the text copy checked.

#### Rationale

The audit (docs/research/28, §2.3, §2.3.1 and §5.1) found the skill layer instructing values the code rejects, in both directions. `kiwi-srs` sets a new requirement's status to a value that is not in the enum, which is the input side of FR-NODE-198; and its conflict branch calls `update_status` with a stability value, which `update-status.ts:106` has always refused, so that instruction has never once succeeded. A 2026-08-26 sweep found the mirror-image defect the audit missed: `kiwi-srs-sync` names a status value as a stability transition. A five-member decision committee reached the axis question unanimously — the conflict hold belongs on Stability, not Status — and the repository's own text already said so in three places, including a recommendation row that reads back the demotion as a stability change and a caution line naming it draft demote. What the committee overturned was this plan's earlier judgement that the branch needed redesign; the trailing clause it rested on turned out to be copied from the adjacent update branch, where it is correct because that branch does name a real status value. The lasting fix is not the four edits but the contract test, because the repository has already repaired this class of defect once by changing data while leaving the text that dictates it untouched.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: No requirement-status slot in any of the three renderings holds a value outside `REQUIREMENT_STATUSES`, and no requirement-stability slot holds a value outside `STABILITY_LEVELS`. Slots are identified by reading the surrounding text, not by matching a single token: the same word appears in identifier fragments, output paths and ordinary prose, and those are left alone.
- [x] AC-2: A test in `test/skills/` walks all three renderings and fails when a status or stability slot names a value the code does not define. It asserts each rendering file was actually read, because the shared reader folds a missing file to an empty string and a check over nothing passes for the same reason a clean one does. A copy of this contract living in the package's own code MAY be left out of the frozen inventory AC-11 requires, but only where another requirement PINS it mechanically: `FR-MCP-060` AC-8 holds the closed value list an MCP tool description presents against the runtime constant that tool's own guard decides by, in both directions, so `update_status` and `update_stability` cannot drift from `REQUIREMENT_STATUSES` and `STABILITY_LEVELS` unobserved. That exemption SHALL be checked for SOUNDNESS as well as for liveness, and the soundness check SHALL be that same comparison made HERE rather than a reference to the requirement that makes it elsewhere, so the excuse does not rest on another file's assertions still running. It SHALL therefore hold only while the presented list equals the enum in both directions: a description that drops its list, invents a value its guard refuses, or withholds one its guard admits stops being exempt and lands back in the inventory. The test SHALL assert that every exemption still claims a site, SHALL freeze WHICH copies are excused so that a further description beginning to restate an enum fails rather than being waved through in silence, and SHALL assert over constructed samples that a copy dropping any one of those properties is not excused. The three descriptions that name a lifecycle value inside a guard clause rather than as a list are pinned by nothing and are frozen in the inventory like every other copy.
- [x] AC-3: The conflict branch of `kiwi-srs` calls `update_stability` rather than `update_status`, and its text carries five things: the tool name, that `Status` is left alone, that `status: "draft"` is refused by `update_status` with `USAGE`, that `reason` writes the Change Notes row so no separate entry is made, and what to do when REQ-X is already `verified` — that call is refused with `MUTATION_DENIED`, so the demotion is not attempted and the conflict is carried by the `conflicts_with` trace link and the user report instead.
- [x] AC-4: `update_stability` is listed in the skill's MCP/CLI tool table and in its section on which mutations speckiwi performs as a single line patch. Absent from the second list, an agent falls back to a hand-written `Edit` and breaks the rule that section exists to state.
- [x] AC-5: The `kiwi-srs-feasibility` status branch either covers `REQUIREMENT_STATUSES` in full or states what it does with the values it does not cover, and its filter list no longer mixes a stability value into a status predicate.
- [x] AC-6: The `kiwi-srs-sync` mutation list no longer names a status value as a stability transition. This is the same defect as the conflict branch with the axes swapped, and it is fixed in the same change so that one repair does not leave its mirror image standing.
- [x] AC-7: `speckiwi skills mirror --check` reports zero divergence, and `.agents/skills/**` was regenerated by `mirror --write` rather than edited by hand.
- [x] AC-8: The contract test reads the shipped text on three anchors, and each anchor is derived from code rather than restated beside it: the two enums for a value that CHANGED, the MCP tool schema for a wrong value that APPEARED beside a call, and a recorded set of (value, file, surrounding text) for a value that MOVED. The test SHALL fail when any anchor stops being derived — when the tool set is written as a literal, when a value floor loses a member the enums still define, or when the recorded site set no longer covers every enum member.
- [x] AC-9: The edge the layers cannot reach SHALL be recorded here as what actually remains, in both directions: the record SHALL NOT depend on an exemption list staying as it is, and it SHALL NOT claim more than is true. Three things remain. (1) A word reaches an agent unread only when four qualifiers hold at once: it names no member of either enum, so no count falls and no site is recorded; it is more than two edits from every member; it is none of the words the blocklist names; and no axis surface, MCP tool or CLI subcommand, stands within the measured window of it. `라운드가 끝나면 REQ 를 shipped 로 올린다` is such a line. The test SHALL hold that line as an executable statement and SHALL assert, for EACH qualifier, a counterexample that drops that qualifier alone and IS read — on a token other than the one the edge names, because a twin built from the same word proves only that the layer is alive for that word. The three sentences an earlier wording of this criterion left out — a legitimate enum word written into the requirement's own Status or Stability field, a misspelling whose axis word stands behind it in Korean word order, and another tool's argument name handed to `update_status` — are among those counterexamples. (2) A rule an acceptance criterion names can be repealed BY REFERENCE, by a sentence that carries none of its words. That is NOT blocked and SHALL NOT be recorded as blocked; it is made visible. The conflict branch's golden fires in all four renderings when the repeal is written and the golden is not regenerated, and when it is regenerated the repeal is one line of a thirteen-line golden diff; the shape of each other section these criteria name is frozen so a repeal paragraph there fails rather than passing in silence. (3) A rule stated in prose that NO acceptance criterion names — a safety gate inverted where no value stands — is outside this requirement, whose Requirement clause is about the values the shipped text names, and SHALL NOT be claimed here.
- [x] AC-10: Every exclusion the contract test applies SHALL be checked for SOUNDNESS as well as for liveness. Liveness asks whether an entry still claims an occurrence; soundness asks whether anything it claims stands where a wrong value could stand, and an exclusion that silences such a place is too wide however alive it is. Three exclusions carry this. The homonym dictionary SHALL NOT speak where the requirement's own Status or Stability field is assigning the value, and the test SHALL assert that no entry does so in the shipped tree. The recorded site set SHALL record EVERY occurrence of every enum member together with the dictionary entry that speaks for it, so that widening the dictionary moves a line in the golden rather than removing it. The exemption applied beside a lifecycle call SHALL be that call's own vocabulary — the argument names its schema entry declares and the axis subcommands' own arguments — rather than every argument name, subcommand and option any tool in the package declares, which admitted `acknowledged`, `applied`, `resolution`, `promote`, `freeze` and `close` into the most explicit value position this corpus has.
- [x] AC-11: The corpus SHALL be every place this package puts contract-carrying text in front of an agent, decided by derivation rather than by a list. The renderings SHALL be read off the disk — every directory under `skills/` plus the mirror — so a rendering added to the tree is swept rather than waiting to be typed into a literal, and the test SHALL fail when a rendering has no floor. The agent instruction block `speckiwi init` writes into a consumer repository is a copy of this contract that no rendering carries; it SHALL be rendered and swept by the same readers. A source file carrying agent-facing text that names an axis and a lifecycle value SHALL be detected by derivation, and the inventory of such files SHALL be frozen so that a further copy fails rather than joining the others unremarked.
- [x] AC-12: The recorded site set makes a commit's newly written value sites finite and complete, and that is worth nothing unless something reads it. A renaming of one file rewrites dozens of recorded lines, and lines an attack added are not distinguishable from them by eye — but they are mechanically, because a renamed occurrence pairs with its own deletion on everything except the file column and a new one pairs with nothing. The repository SHALL carry a tool that performs that pairing and prints the unpaired additions, and the test SHALL exercise the tool's pairing so the defence does not rest on a script nobody runs.

#### Requirement

The append path that guards `.kiwi/waves.jsonl` SHALL validate the prospective journal under the engine of the line being appended rather than under a literal engine, so that a contract-violating terminal line is refused on every engine the journal carries and not only on one — at the write, and at the `--dry-run` preview that precedes it. The shipped `kiwi-orchestrator` skill SHALL name the validator that performs this refusal, when to call it, what to call it with, which of its two callers can judge a wave-master journal at all, and what to do when it refuses, in every rendering it ships. The shared journal contract that skill names as its event SSOT SHALL NOT rule on that procedure, so the instruction cannot be contradicted from the one file the skill itself defers to. This closes the gap for a line that reaches `orchestrate journal append`: the guard exists, is wired, and is described in the skill text as refusing malformed terminal lines, while a line written under any other engine was never in the set that check read. Two remainders are named here rather than claimed as closed — FR-FLOW-156 owns the wave-master emit path that bypasses the tool altogether, and FR-NODE-199 owns the callers that can still empty the candidate set through their own arguments. That instruction lives in the second of the two subsections `FR-FLOW-157` splits `§V.final-verify` into — the one whose heading declares this requirement as its owner, holding the terminal line and the validator that judges it — and an edit that lands in the first, which `FR-FLOW-131` owns, is judged by that requirement rather than by this one.

#### Rationale

The audit (docs/research/28, §3.6 and §3.7) reported that no skill calls the journal validator. That report was half wrong and the correction matters more than the original finding: `orchestrate_journal_append` already validates the prospective journal and refuses an error-severity result, so on the orchestrator engine a malformed terminal line never lands. The defect is narrower and worse — the parse that feeds that check pins `engine: "kiwi-orchestrator"`, and the parser skips lines of any other engine. For a wave-master run the candidate set is empty, an empty set raises no diagnostics, and the write is accepted. The skill text meanwhile states that the validator refuses such lines, which is true on one engine and false on the other. A guard believed to be there is worse than a guard known to be absent. Measured at the time of writing: `orchestrate_validate` appears zero times across all four renderings, and `validate-spec-error` is declared by `kiwi-srs-sync` alone.
- [2026-08-27] Scope correction (2026-08-27, first verification round): the causal sentence above holds for a line that reaches `orchestrate journal append`. The shipped `kiwi-wave-master` does not reach it - `_shared/kiwi/waves-event.md` section 5 tells it to emit with a shell redirect - so this requirement covers the tool path only. FR-FLOW-156 owns that bypass. FR-NODE-199 owns the MCP validator, which takes no engine, and the run-id axis, which empties the same candidate set.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: A terminal line whose `engine` is not `kiwi-orchestrator` and which omits `terminal_review` is refused at append with no bytes reaching the journal, and is refused identically under `--dry-run`, which is the only judgement an agent sees before it writes. The same payload under `kiwi-orchestrator` is refused today and is asserted alongside it on both paths as the control, so the red proves the engine was the cause rather than the payload; a discharging payload is accepted on both paths, so a fix that refused everything fails too.
- [x] AC-2: The engine passed to the prospective-journal parse is derived from the payload by the resolver the parser itself uses, not restated beside it, and both parses in that function — the preview and the write — receive that one resolution. The second half is asserted over the function's source text, because a restatement that is correct today is behaviourally identical to the resolver it copies and no run can tell them apart. A second spelling of that rule is a second place to drift.
- [x] AC-3: Every rendering of `kiwi-orchestrator` — the three variants and the mirror — names the validator in its terminal-verify section: when it is called (immediately after the terminal line is written), what is called (the MCP tool with the arguments it takes, the CLI fallback, and the engine flag), which caller can judge a wave-master journal at all (the CLI only, because the MCP binding declares no engine and defaults to `kiwi-orchestrator`), and what happens on refusal (halt on the named gate, do not rewrite the terminal line). The call sits within one window AFTER the terminal-review contract paragraph, keyed on a signature the instruction does not reproduce, so an instruction parked elsewhere fails. `FR-FLOW-157` splits `§V.final-verify` in two, and the subsection whose heading declares THIS requirement as its owner is held byte-exact from its heading to its end against a checked-in golden in all four renderings, so every clause inside it is covered to one depth: a presence assertion is satisfied by its own inversion, and the clause a probe last reached must not be the only one defended. Inside that section no sentence permits the rewrite the refusal branch forbids or retires the rule, so an inversion preserving every token is refused as well as a deletion. The closed subject vocabulary this criterion formerly placed over the section's front half is REMOVED with the split, measured on both sides. It closed spellings rather than the subject: `mcp`, the full-width `ＭＣＰ`, `orchestrate-validate` and `run_id` each carried a routing-rule contradiction past every assertion. And it refused seven legitimate `FR-FLOW-131` edits, among them adding `--strict-grounding` — a flag this skill's own options table defines — to the review hop's argument fence; all seven are measured green after the split. What the removal gives up is recorded in AC-4 and asserted by `FR-FLOW-157` AC-5. `kiwi-wave-master`'s own renderings are outside this criterion; `FR-FLOW-156` owns them.
- [x] AC-4: The contract test states what it does and does not guarantee, measured rather than asserted from reading. It guarantees presence in every rendering. It does NOT guarantee that an agent calls the tool. Outside the compared section it does NOT catch a contradiction, and after `FR-FLOW-157`'s split that outside includes the review-hop half of `§V.final-verify` itself — the price of the boundary, taken because the vocabulary it replaces closed spellings rather than the subject and refused seven legitimate `FR-FLOW-131` edits. Such a contradiction may sit ANYWHERE outside the compared section, not only above its heading: measured, `§V.emit-and-finish`, `§V.halt` and the review-hop section each accept a retraction written with every name this instruction uses, as does a second, differently-spelled mention of the tool: nothing here reads the rest of the document. A probe naming the terminal line by pronoun with a verb OUTSIDE the closed rewrite list fails the comparison inside the section and passes every other mechanism outside it. Three coordinated-edit shapes are accepted cost, not closed holes; each was measured to green, because they do not cost the same. Inverting one of the six NAMED clauses takes four file kinds — the body, the golden, that clause's ledger rows, and THIS test, whose presence and hedge assertions refuse the weakened sentence after the other three agree — and the rows make the diff name the rule. APPENDING a permitting sentence inside the compared section takes the body and the golden alone, because a row pins the bytes of the clause it quotes and sees nothing added beside it; measured green against both polarity bans. Deleting a ledger row buys silence, not a cheaper edit: its id is declared in three test files, so the rows come out only with those declarations, and the clause still sits inside the compared section, so the inversion then costs the body, the golden and this test on top. Unstated, the next reader takes the green as evidence of them.
- [x] AC-5: The wording introduced by this requirement is counted in the shipped tree before the change and recorded as zero, so a test that would have passed on the old text cannot be mistaken for one that holds the new rule. A token that was NOT zero is recorded with what it actually was and where, so the record cannot be read as a clean sweep it was not.
- [x] AC-6: `speckiwi skills mirror --check` reports zero divergence. Provenance is deliberately not an acceptance criterion: a mirror hand-edited into the same bytes is indistinguishable from a regenerated one in the artifact, so `regenerated rather than hand-edited` is recorded as method in the Implementation Notes with the numstat that shows it. What that gives up: a hand-edited mirror matching byte for byte passes this criterion.
- [x] AC-7: This requirement does not claim that a run which never wrote a terminal line is caught, nor that every line present in the file is judged. The rules fire on the lines the parse ADMITS, and the parse filters by run id and engine together. Measured: an absent line raises nothing; a present line is invisible when its `run_id` differs from the one the reader was given, when it does not CLOSE THE RUN, or when its `schema_version` is below 1.5.0. Closing the run is not the `final-verify` phase alone: `closesTheRun` admits a delegated-complete dispatch result too, because R-STEP and R-PLAN terminate there and never write a `final-verify` line, so a rule keyed on the phase would police one rung of three - measured, such a line IS judged and raises `terminal-review-loop-missing`. Each axis is recorded here with its owner rather than left to be found in a run that passed while doing nothing. `run_id` is owned by FR-NODE-199 AC-2 and the MCP engine axis by FR-NODE-199 AC-1. The close axis is a DEFENDED exclusion and not a hole: a line that closes nothing also leaves the run open, and `computeRunProgress` then reports `runComplete` false and `needsFinalVerify` true - measured on a two-line run - so no false completion is produced, exactly as a `status` other than `complete` behaves. The `schema_version` axis is the one that does produce a false completion: measured on the same run, stamping the close 1.4.0 silences the diagnostic while `runComplete` stays true. It is deliberate and already recorded in code, not unowned - the rule is judged at each line's own version to keep the event contract's additivity guarantee, and `src/core/orchestrator/waves-validate.ts:392-406` records the remedy that was implemented, went red on the retroactivity case and was reverted. Unlike the 1.1.0 and 1.2.0 gates, the event contract's run-scoped downgrade guard is deliberately not applied here. That decision belongs to FR-NODE-188's version scope, not to this requirement and not to FR-NODE-199.
- [x] AC-8: The file `§0.1` of the skill names as the journal's event SSOT - `_shared/kiwi/waves-event.md`, in all four renderings - does not rule on this procedure. That section gives the file its schema, location and `complete` rules, so when the terminal line is validated, by which caller, and what happens on refusal belong to `§V.final-verify`. The five names by which a sentence can rule on that - the MCP tool, `validateWavesJournal`, the gate it raises, `--engine`, and the common noun `검증기` - are measured at zero in that file and asserted to stay zero, and the rewrite ban reads it. Measured before: such a sentence in all four renderings left every assertion under `test/skills/` green and the mirror clean. What this does NOT cover runs in two directions, both measured when written and both since taken by `FR-FLOW-158`. Across files: `§0` defers to ten shared files and this criterion covers the one `§0.1` names, not the other nine - `run-ledger.md` (`§0.10`, the SSOT for the journal's write discipline) was uncovered, a sentence there using all five names and letting the line off left the three suites green, and `verify-loop.md` (`§0.7`) did the same. Within the covered file: five is the WIDEST set it can carry, not the set that closes it - it writes the bare noun `검증` 27 times legitimately, so only `검증기` could be banned and a sentence built from `검증` alone was measured green inside it. `FR-FLOW-158`'s suite now sweeps all of `_shared/kiwi/` for those names, closing the first remainder, and bans the shape that lets the line off, closing the second for the shapes AC-5's verb list carries. This criterion reaches only the one file, five classes stay green inside it, the five `FR-FLOW-158` AC-6 enumerates and counts - another conjugation outside the three slots, the polite register, a verb derived from a root it carries, a synonym or the pronoun form, and a slot spelled with a space the list does not write - and a contradiction planted outside `_shared/kiwi/` is outside both.

### FR-FLOW-156 — The wave-master run writes its journal through the guarded append tool instead of a shell redirect

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 3.1.0 |
| Status | planned |
| Priority | high |
| Tags | plan-3.0-04b, audit-28, follow-up-fr-flow-155 |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | docs/plan/3.0/04.orchestrate-gate-wiring.md, docs/research/28.skills-mcp-end-to-end-audit.md |

#### Requirement

The shared waves-event emit pattern SHALL write `.kiwi/waves.jsonl` through `orchestrate journal append` rather than a shell redirect, so that the terminal-line refusal wired into that tool applies to the run family whose terminal line it was wired for. `kiwi-wave-master` SHALL name that tool in every rendering it ships and SHALL forbid a direct append, as `kiwi-orchestrator` already does. The `writer` stamp SHALL be applied by the tool rather than hand-written into the emit template, because a hand-written stamp makes a bypassing write indistinguishable from a guarded one under `--strict`.

#### Rationale

FR-FLOW-155 made the append guard read the engine of the line being appended, which makes the refusal reach a `kiwi-wave-master` line that passes through the tool. Its verification then found that the shipped `kiwi-wave-master` never passes through the tool. `orchestrate journal append` is named by `kiwi-orchestrator` alone; the shared SSOT `_shared/kiwi/waves-event.md` section 5 tells every other caller to emit with `echo '{...}' >> "$WAVE_DIR/waves.jsonl"`, and the third of those three lines is the run-scope terminal line that carries `terminal_review`. That template also hard-codes the writer stamp, so the unstamped-writer check cannot separate the bypass from a tool write. The result is the shape this project has already named the worst one: `kiwi-wave-master/SKILL.md` states that the validator refuses a terminal line missing those fields, and on the path that skill actually instructs, nothing refuses it. Closing this needs a decision the emit pattern currently forecloses - the same section ends with "emit is best-effort, a failure must not fail the orchestration", which cannot survive a write that is allowed to refuse.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC-1: Section 5 of `_shared/kiwi/waves-event.md` emits through the append tool rather than a shell redirect, in all three renderings, and the run-scope terminal line is one of the lines it covers. Measured before the change: three `echo ... >> "$WAVE_DIR/waves.jsonl"` templates, the third carrying `terminal_review`.
- [ ] AC-2: The `writer` field is applied by the tool and no longer hard-coded in the emit template, so a line written outside the tool is distinguishable under `--strict`. Measured before the change: the template writes `"writer":"speckiwi-orchestrate/{pkgVersion}"` by hand, which the unstamped check accepts.
- [ ] AC-3: `kiwi-wave-master` names the append tool and forbids a direct append in every rendering it ships. That is three renderings, not four: the mirror excludes this skill, and a test that assumes four here is asserting over a file that does not exist.
- [ ] AC-4: The conflict between a guarded write that can refuse and the emit pattern's `best-effort` clause is resolved in the text rather than left to the implementer, and the resolution is recorded in this requirement. A refused terminal line halts the run on its gate; it is not an emit failure to swallow.
- [ ] AC-5: A run whose terminal line is refused is observable after the fact - the refusal is recorded somewhere a later reader can find - because a halt that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from a run that was never started.

### FR-FLOW-157 — §V.final-verify is split so the review hop and the terminal-line verification each own a section, and the second is held whole against a golden

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Type | functional |
| Target | 3.1.0 |
| Status | verified |
| Priority | high |
| Tags | plan-3.0-04b, audit-28, follow-up-fr-flow-155 |
| Risk | medium |
| Stability | evolving |
| Verification Method | test |
| GitHub Issue | - |
| Related Docs | docs/plan/3.0/04.orchestrate-gate-wiring.md, docs/research/28.skills-mcp-end-to-end-audit.md |

#### Requirement

`kiwi-orchestrator`'s `§V.final-verify` SHALL be split into two sections in every rendering it ships - one owning the run-window review hop that `FR-FLOW-131` governs, one owning the terminal line and the validator that judges it, which `FR-FLOW-155` governs - and the second SHALL be held byte-exact against a checked-in golden from its heading to its end, so that no clause of it is read only by a lexical rule. The closed subject vocabulary `FR-FLOW-155` AC-3 placed over the front half SHALL be removed in the same change, because after the split the text it guards is no longer in the section whose rules it could contradict. The ownership boundary SHALL be restated in both requirements, so a later edit is judged by the requirement that owns the section it lands in.

#### Rationale

One section carries two subjects while two requirements own it, so no byte comparison can be drawn across it: freezing the whole section would fail `FR-FLOW-131`'s own edits under a message about a terminal-line contract, and freezing half of it leaves the other half to lexical rules. `FR-FLOW-155`'s verification measured what those lexical rules buy and what they cost, and both measurements point at the same repair. On the defence side they close spellings rather than the subject - `mcp`, the full-width `ＭＣＰ`, `M C P`, `orchestrate-validate` and `run_id`, the last being the journal schema's own spelling of the run id, each carried a contradiction of the routing rule past every assertion, and four plain-Korean inversions carrying none of the eleven nouns did the same to the immediate-validation, routing, engine-flag and halting clauses. On the cost side seven legitimate edits to the review hop were measured and all seven turn red with none worth the refusal; one of them adds `--strict-grounding`, a flag this same skill defines in its own options table, to the review hop's argument fence, where the failure message forbids both available repairs at once. A section boundary is what those lexical rules are trying to substitute for.

#### Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC-1: `§V.final-verify` is two sections in all four renderings after the change, the second beginning at the terminal-review contract signature the golden currently keys on, and the ownership of each is stated in its own text rather than inferred from the requirement that reads it. No prose sits outside the two, so every byte of the section has an owner: the section's recovery-class line, which `FR-FLOW-074` AC-2 reads, moves under the first heading rather than staying above both, where it belonged to neither requirement and a retraction planted beside it was measured green. Measured before the change through the reader the suites use: one section of 1924 characters in which the compared span begins 832 characters in - 43% of the section read by no byte comparison.
- [x] AC-2: The terminal-line section is compared byte-exact against a checked-in golden from its heading to its end in all four renderings. Three edit shapes are each measured red separately rather than assumed: deleting one sentence, appending one permitting sentence, and reordering two sentences without changing a byte of either. Each is planted in a rendering and read back through the extraction the live comparison uses, not spliced into the fixture, so a reader that learned to swallow one of the shapes is caught here rather than passed. A rendering whose section matches the golden is green, so a comparison that refused everything fails too.
- [x] AC-3: No lexical rule over text `FR-FLOW-131` owns survives in this requirement's suite. The seven edits the closed vocabulary refused are each measured green after the change: adding `--strict-grounding` to the review hop's argument fence, naming `kiwi-wave-master`'s wave-window convention for contrast, recording a round through the MCP tool `orchestrate_round_record`, calling the review's output `진단`, calling a child's regression result `검증`, passing `--run-id {run_id}` on resume, and naming the CLI as the fallback when the Skill call is unavailable. Each is reverted after measurement; what is kept is the measurement, not the edit.
- [x] AC-4: The rules the split moves are not weakened by moving. Each of the six clauses `FR-FLOW-155`'s ledger names is still refused when inverted inside the new section, the rows are re-pointed at that section rather than deleted, and the rule-id set the requirement owns stays frozen so a clause cannot be released by deleting its row instead of editing it.
- [x] AC-5: What this requirement does NOT guarantee, each recorded because it was measured rather than inferred. (a) It does not catch a contradiction placed in another section of the same file: the section immediately following, `§V.emit-and-finish`, and `§V.halt` were both measured accepting a retraction that uses every banned noun, and a whole-section golden reads one section. After the split the review-hop section JOINS that set - a sentence there saying the terminal line's validation is optional is compared by nothing - and so does a second mention of the tool spelled differently from the one the golden freezes, which `FR-FLOW-155` had stopped asserting on the ground that eleven banned nouns held that half; this requirement removed those nouns, so that ground went with them. Both are asserted here as measurements, and that is the price of drawing the boundary at a section, recorded rather than left for the next reader to find. (b) It does not guarantee that an agent calls the tool; that limit is `FR-FLOW-155` AC-4's and is unchanged. (c) It does not reach `_shared/kiwi/**`, which `FR-FLOW-158` owns. (d) It does not close the coordinated edit: changing the body and the golden together still lands, and a ledger row raises that to four file kinds only for the clause it names.
